title: Reverse an array (swap first with last, second with second-last, using two pointers).

s1_definition.profdef: Reversing an array in place uses the two-pointer technique. One pointer starts at the left end and one at the right end; you swap the two elements, then move the left pointer right and the right pointer left, stopping when they meet in the middle. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space because you only swap, never allocate a second array.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh has a printed statement where transactions are listed oldest first, but he wants newest first. He puts one finger on the top line and one on the bottom line, swaps those two lines, then moves both fingers inward by one and swaps again. He keeps going until his fingers meet in the middle. Now the whole statement is reversed without needing a second sheet of paper.
s1_definition.oneliner: Swap the two ends and move inward with two pointers until they meet, reversing the array in place.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Reversing an array in place uses the two-pointer technique. One pointer starts at the left end and one at the right end; you swap the two elements, then move the left pointer right and the right pointer left, stopping when they meet in the middle. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space because you only swap, never allocate a second array.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh has a printed statement where transactions are listed oldest first, but he wants newest first. He puts one finger on the top line and one on the bottom line, swaps those two lines, then moves both fingers inward by one and swaps again. He keeps going until his fingers meet in the middle. Now the whole statement is reversed without needing a second sheet of paper.

**One line to remember:** Swap the two ends and move inward with two pointers until they meet, reversing the array in place.

sections.s2_technical:
The two-pointer approach uses `left` starting at index 0 and `right` starting at the last index. In each step you swap `array[left]` and `array[right]`, then do `left++` and `right--`. You continue while `left < right`. When they meet or cross, every element has been placed in its mirrored position.

In-place reversal is important because it uses O(1) extra space. You only need one temporary variable to hold a value during the swap. The alternative of building a new reversed array uses O(n) extra space, which is wasteful for large statements.

The loop runs n/2 times because each iteration fixes two elements, so the time is O(n). A single middle element in an odd-length array stays in place and needs no swap, which the `left < right` condition handles automatically. This works for any element type — here we reverse `BigDecimal` transaction amounts.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India stores Rajesh's transactions oldest first in the database, but the mobile app must display newest first so he sees recent activity at the top. The system must reverse the list of amounts. This is exactly how the two-pointer reversal works — swap the ends and move inward.

Problem 2 — The app runs on phones with limited memory, so we should reverse in place rather than allocating a second array. This is exactly why we use the in-place two-pointer swap, which needs only one temporary variable.

The code has an `Account` holding amounts in an array, and a `StatementReverser` class with a `reverseInPlace` method. The demo reverses Rajesh's amounts and logs before and after.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: amounts `[1000, 2000, 3000, 4000]`, with `left=0` and `right=3`.

Step 1 — Swap index 0 and index 3. Array becomes `[4000, 2000, 3000, 1000]`. Move `left` to 1, `right` to 2.

Step 2 — `left=1 < right=2`, so swap index 1 and index 2. Array becomes `[4000, 3000, 2000, 1000]`. Move `left` to 2, `right` to 1.

Step 3 — Now `left=2` is not less than `right=1`, so the loop stops. The array is fully reversed.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Before (oldest first): [1000.00, 2000.00, 3000.00, 4000.00]
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] After (newest first):  [4000.00, 3000.00, 2000.00, 1000.00]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Input: [1000, 2000, 3000, 4000]   left=0 right=3
    │
    ▼
  StatementReverser.reverseInPlace()
    │ swap(0,3): [4000, 2000, 3000, 1000]  left=1 right=2
    │ swap(1,2): [4000, 3000, 2000, 1000]  left=2 right=1
    │ left >= right → stop
    ▼
  Array reversed in place (O(1) extra space)
    │
    ▼
  Log: "After (newest first): [4000, 3000, 2000, 1000]"
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Reversing an array is a textbook two-pointer problem that I solve in place. I put one pointer at the left end and one at the right end, swap the two elements they point at, then move the left pointer one step right and the right pointer one step left. I keep going while the left pointer is still before the right pointer. When they meet in the middle, the whole array is reversed. The loop runs about half the length of the array, so it is linear time, and because I only use a single temporary variable for the swap, it is constant extra space.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this when displaying statements. The database stores Rajesh's transactions oldest first, but the mobile app needs to show the newest transactions at the top. Rather than issuing a second expensive sorted query or building a whole new array, I reverse the list in place inside the service layer.

The in-place aspect is the part I emphasise in an interview, because the naive solution is to create a brand new array and copy elements into it backwards, which doubles the memory. On a phone displaying a long statement that extra memory matters, so the two-pointer swap that needs only one temporary variable is the professional choice. An odd-length array handles itself automatically, because when the two pointers land on the same middle element the condition stops the loop and that single element correctly stays in place.
